item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony Powers Red Sox Past Rays, Closer To Playoff Berth originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox spent much of Friday night walking a tightrope. Roman Anthony made sure they had enough of a cushion to survive. Anthony homered and drove in three runs, Ranger Suárez battled through 5 2/3 innings and the Red Sox held on for a 4-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field.
Boston improved to 84-70 with its second consecutive victory and snapped Tampa Bay's six-game winning streak. The Red Sox entered the series opener with a magic number of three to clinch an American League wild-card berth and could secure their postseason spot as early as Saturday.
It was not a comfortable victory.
Red Sox pitchers issued nine walks, including four over the final four innings. The Rays loaded the bases in both the sixth and ninth but went 0-for-13 with runners in scoring position and stranded 12 runners. Erik Miller finally ended the ninth-inning adventure by getting Chandler Simpson to ground out with the bases loaded.
Here are three takeaways from Boston's important victory.
Roman Anthony Sets Tone Immediately
Anthony did not wait long to make his presence felt. The Red Sox rookie crushed Ian Seymour's third pitch of the game 438 feet to center field, giving Boston a 1-0 lead before most of the announced crowd of 23,342 had settled into its seats.
It was Anthony's fifth home run of the season and the third leadoff homer of his young career. The Rays answered in the bottom of the first when Junior Caminero drove in Yandy Díaz with a groundout, but Anthony struck again one inning later.
Trevor Story singled and Caleb Durbin followed with another base hit. After Nate Eaton walked to load the bases, Anthony delivered a two-out single to right that scored Story and Durbin. Anthony finished 2-for-5 with three RBIs, accounting for nearly all of Boston's offense on one of the biggest nights of its season.
Jahmai Jones supplied the other run by launching a 414-foot solo homer to left in the third inning. Jones' sixth home run gave Boston a 4-1 advantage that held until the ninth.
Ranger Suárez Bends Without Breaking
Suárez rarely had a clean inning, but the left-hander consistently found his way out of trouble. The Boston starter allowed only three hits and one run while striking out five. He also issued five walks and needed 98 pitches to record 17 outs.
His best defensive moment came in the fourth inning.
Taylor Walls hit a 100-mph line drive directly back at Suárez, who made the catch before throwing to first base to double off Nick Fortes. The play erased a scoring opportunity and helped Suárez navigate another stressful inning. The left-hander improved to 8-4 and lowered his ERA to 3.27.
Wyatt Olds entered with two outs in the sixth and immediately made matters worse by issuing two walks. He recovered to strike out Jake Fraley with the bases loaded, preserving Boston's three-run advantage.
Greg Weissert provided the calmest portion of the night, allowing one hit over two scoreless innings.
Erik Miller Survives Chaotic Ninth Inning
The Red Sox carried a 4-1 lead into the ninth, but Miller turned the final three outs into a full-blown ordeal. The left-hander issued two walks and threw three wild pitches during a 32-pitch inning. Jonathan Aranda drove in one run with a fielder's choice, cutting Boston's lead to 4-2.
Tampa Bay eventually loaded the bases with two outs, bringing Simpson to the plate as the potential winning run. Miller induced a ground ball to third baseman Durbin, who completed the force play at second to end the game. Miller earned his fifth save despite allowing one run, one hit and two walks.
Boston will take the victory, especially at this stage of the season, but the nine walks gave the club another issue to clean up before October. The Red Sox will attempt to clinch their postseason berth Saturday when they continue the three-game series in Tampa Bay. The Rays are scheduled to start right-hander Freddy Peralta, while Boston has yet to announce it's starter.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Red Sox’ Ranger Suarez sets a career high in walks, but navigates tightrope in win
item.dc:creator: Sean McAdam
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all. There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings. But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough. "I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had
item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — It was by no means a textbook display of pitching. There were walks in each of the first four innings, and a career-high five in all.
There were deep counts, lots of traffic and 98 pitches required in fewer than six innings.
But what counts most is not the strikes or the 1-2-3 innings, but the final score. So a taut 4-2 victory for the Red Sox over the Tampa Bay Rays was, especially at this time of year, reward enough.
"I think it was OK," shrugged Suarez afterward. "I had traffic every single inning because of the walks, but I was able to limit damage today and that was part of it."
Suarez had difficulty explaining how the walks piled up on him. It wasn't mechanical, and it wasn't the result of nibbling around the strike zone.
"I think it was one of those nights when I didn't have the command," he said. "But I was able to get outs when I needed."
The latter has always been his calling card. In an era when most starters unleash fastballs at 95 mph or better, Suarez thrives by mixing pitches, keeping hitters off balance and inducing soft contact.
On nights when he can't locate with precision, the margin for error slips further. But again, knowing how to get out of trouble is a mound skill in and of itself.
Suarez has used that talent particularly well in the postseason before, which is part of what motivated the Red Sox to offer him $130 million over five years last winter. Suarez isn't about to come unglued in Yankee Stadium in two weeks — or any other time he gets the ball in the postseason. His career ERA of 1.48 in the playoffs virtually guarantees that.
"He was very competitive with men on base," said interim manager Chad Tracy. "He lost some counts, was behind more counts today, but he wa able to really good pitches with people on base."
Even as he labored, Suarez was adding to a September resumé which has him 3-0 with 0.92 ERA in his last three outings while limiting opposing hitters to a .186 batting average.
No one knows exactly how or when Suarez will fit into Boston's postseason rotation. The assumption is that Sonny Gray will pitch Game 1, with either Payton Tolle or Suarez slotted for Game 2, and the remaining choice available for a winner-take-all Game 3.
Of course, the risk there is that a team may never get to its third starter if it doesn't win at least one of the first two games. That's part of the difficult decision the Red Sox will have to make before their wild card round gets underway.
Even with his history of success in October, Suarez isn't thinking too much about the postseason — not yet anyway.
"No, no,'' he said with a chuckle. "When we clinch, I'll be able to do that. But mathematically, we're not there yet, so I'm not thinking about that."
Suarez has one more start in the regular season, which he can treat as both a tuneup for himself and an audition for Game 2 in the best-of-three wild card round.,
"He's a very good competitor, a good pitcher that even when he gets traffic, you trust that he's going to find his way through it. He does that at times this year, so that's never a concern with him."

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Roman Anthony homered and drove in three runs and the Boston Red Sox took a big step toward clinching an American League playoff spot with a 4-2 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday night.
The Red Sox, who entered Friday with a magic number of three, could secure a wild-card spot as early as Saturday.
Junior Caminero and Jonathan Aranda drove in runs for the post-season-bound Rays. They had won six in a row.
Anthony hit the game’s third pitch from Ian Seymour (9-7) into the right-field seats for his third career leadoff homer. Then, in the second inning, Anthony broke a 1-1 tie and drove in two more runs with a two-out single.
Jahmai Jones gave Boston a 4-1 advantage with his own solo homer to lead off the third. Caleb Durbin added two hits for the Red Sox, who own the American League’s third-best record (84-70), behind the Rays and Yankees.
Red Sox starter Ranger Suarez (8-4) threw 5 2/3 innings, allowing three hits and one run with five walks and five strikeouts. He also snared Taylor Walls’ 100-mph liner in the fourth, before completing an inning-ending double play.
Tampa Bay couldn’t capitalize on multiple opportunities, including nine Red Sox walks. The Rays left the bases loaded in the sixth and ninth, when Erik Miller retired Chandler Simpson on a game-ending grounder. Tampa Bay was 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position.
Boston left-hander Erik Miller had his fifth save despite a shaky ninth inning, including three wild pitches and two walks.
Up next
Tampa Bay RHP Freddy Peralta (9-11, 4.67 ERA) was set to start Saturday. Boston had yet to announce a starter.

item.content:encoded:
Roman Anthony homered and had three RBIs, Jahmai Jones went deep and the Boston Red Sox cooled off the first-place Tampa Bay Rays with a 4-2 victory on Friday night in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The Red Sox (84-70) opened their final road series of the regular season by scoring all of their runs in the first three innings to win for the second consecutive night.
Anthony went 2-for-5, while Caleb Durbin was 2-for-3 as the team produced nine hits.
Starting pitcher Ranger Suarez (8-4) fought control issues but went 5 2/3 innings in earning the win. He allowed one run on three hits while striking out five and walking five.
Junior Caminero doubled, walked twice and drove in a run for Tampa Bay (93-60), but the American League’s top club had only five hits, was a brutal 0-for-13 with runners in scoring position and had its six-game winning streak snapped.
Starter Ian Seymour (9-7) was hit hard in the first two innings and finished by allowing four runs on seven hits in five frames. He whiffed five and walked two.
On the third pitch of the game, leadoff hitter Anthony crushed a Statcast-estimated 438-foot blast to center field. It was the left fielder’s fifth homer.
Caminero’s RBI groundout tied it in the bottom half, but Anthony did more damage by ripping a two-out single to right for a 3-1 lead in the second.
Jones made it 4-1 leading off the third by lining Seymour’s changeup out to left for his sixth homer.
Suarez got out of a slight jam in the third after Caminero walked and Ryan Vilade singled, but he retired red-hot Chandler Simpson and Jonny DeLuca to maintain the three-run lead.
The home club put together a strong threat in the sixth after Wyatt Olds relieved Suarez and issued two walks to fill the bases with two outs. However, he battled back in the count against pinch hitter Jake Fraley and struck him out.
In the ninth, Jonathan Aranda’s groundout scored a run, but Erik Miller got Simpson to ground out to second with the bases loaded for his fifth save.
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG -- Roman Anthony atacó el tercer pitcheo del juego de la noche del viernes en el Tropicana Field, quizás dejando claro, con un batazo de 438 pies según la proyección de Statcast hacia la corta distancia del jardín derecho-central, que su mala racha ha terminado.
Por si fuera poco, el joven de 22 años volvió al plato un inning después y conectó el primer hit de su carrera en 11 visitas al plato con las bases llenas, un sencillo de dos carreras hacia el jardín derecho.
Anthony fue quien encabezó la ofensiva mientras los Medias Rojas (84-70) se acercaron más a asegurar su boleto a la postemporada con una victoria por 4-2 sobre los Rays, quienes tienen el mejor récord de la Liga Americana con 93-60 y llegaron al encuentro con una racha de seis triunfos consecutivos.
Aunque Anthony estuvo encendido con el bate en sus primeros cuatro juegos tras regresar de la lista de lesionados, sus siguientes 12 encuentros antes del viernes fueron muy distintos: línea ofensiva de .137/.214/.296, con un extrabase en 56 visitas al plato.
Desde la lomita, Ranger Suárez (8-4, EFE de 3.27) completó su tercera apertura sólida consecutiva, pese a otorgar cinco bases por bolas, la mayor cantidad de su carrera. El zurdo logró salir de los problemas que él mismo generó, permitiendo apenas tres hits y una carrera, con cinco ponches en 5.2 innings y 98 pitcheos, 56 de ellos strikes.
Wyatt Olds, quien últimamente ha pasado de ser un llamado sin muchos reflectores a una pieza importante del bullpen, otorgó bases por bolas a los primeros dos bateadores que enfrentó al entrar en lugar de Suárez, pero salió del apuro al ponchar al bateador emergente Jake Fraley.
Greg Weissert respondió con dos innings importantes, en los que sorteó un hit.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – Roman Anthony tore into the third pitch of Friday night’s game at Tropicana Field, perhaps making a Statcast-projected 438-foot statement into a short porch in right-center field that his slump is over.
For good measure, the 22-year-old stepped up an inning later and came up with his first career hit in 11 plate appearances with the bases loaded, bashing a two-run single to right.
It was Anthony leading the offense as the Sox (84-70) pushed closer to punching their ticket to the postseason with a 4-2 victory over the Rays, who have an American League-best 93-60 record and came into this one with a six-game winning streak.
While Anthony swung a hot bat in his first four games back from the injured list, his next 12 games entering Friday went like this: a slash line of .137/.214/.296 with one extra-base hit in 56 plate appearances.
From the mound, Ranger Suarez (8-4, 3.27 ERA) turned in his third consecutive solid start, despite issuing a career-high five walks. The lefty worked around the trouble he created, allowing just three hits and one run while striking out five over 5 2/3 innings and 98 pitches (56 strikes).
Wyatt Olds, who has gone from an unheralded callup to a key bullpen piece of late, walked the first two batters he faced when he came on for Suarez, but he escaped by striking out pinch-hitter Jake Fraley.
Greg Weissert came through with two big innings, working around one hit.

item.content:encoded:
Erik Miller News: Barely secures save against Tampa Bay
Miller earned his fifth save of the season in Friday's 4-2 win over the Rays, allowing one run on one hit and two walks while striking out two in the ninth inning.
With Aroldis Chapman shelved by a lat issue, the Red Sox turned to Miller for the ninth inning to protect the team's 4-1 lead. It turned out to be a dramatic finish for Boston, with Miller tossing two wild pitches in the inning and loading the bases. Luckily for the southpaw, he limited the damage to just one run to secure the win for the Red Sox, who are inching closer toward punching their spot in the American League playoffs. Miller and Garrett Whitlock figure to be the top closer options for the Red Sox for as long as Chapman is sidelined.

item.dc:creator: Peter Abraham
item.description: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Tampa Bay Rays have been the best team in the American League for much of this season, particularly at Tropicana Field. But with one All-Star on the injured list and two others unavailable, the Red Sox came away with a 4-2 victory before a crowd of 23,342 as Roman Anthony drove in three runs. item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Tampa Bay Rays have been the best team in the American League for much of this season, particularly at Tropicana Field.
But with one All-Star on the injured list and two others unavailable, the Red Sox came away with a 4-2 victory before a crowd of 23,342 as Roman Anthony drove in three runs.
Now the magic number to clinch a playoff spot is down to two.
Ranger Suarez (8-4) and three relievers walked nine but held the Rays to five hits. Tampa Bay was hitless in 13 at-bats with runners in scoring position and left 12 men on base.
It was an impressive victory for the Sox, considering the 93-60 Rays are close to clinching the best record in the league and home-field advantage through, at least, the American League Championship Series.
The Sox were without Ceddanne Rafaela, who isn’t expected to come off the injured list until next week. Aroldis Chapman (lat strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) were not available.
With Garrett Whitlock left in the bullpen after pitching Thursday night, the Sox used lefthander Erik Miller to get the final three outs for his first save with the team.
Miller walked two and threw three wild pitches in a wild ninth inning, giving up a run before finally getting Chandler Simpson to ground to second for the final out.
Miller had allowed five runs over 5⅓ innings and put 10 men on base in his previous six appearances.
The Sox didn’t arrive at the team hotel until close to 5 a.m. after beating the Rangers in Texas on Thursday night. The Rays had a day game at home that ended 13 hours earlier. But the Sox had more energy early on.
Anthony blasted the third pitch of the game from Ian Seymour 438 feet to center field for his fifth home run.
Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the second inning with singles. Isiah Kiner-Falefa dropped a bunt to advance the runners before Nate Eaton worked a walk to load the bases.
After Connor Wong struck out, Anthony worked the count full and lined a hard single to right field to drive in two more runs. The three RBIs matched his career high.
Jahmai Jones homered leading off the third inning, a 414-foot shot to left field.
Suarez did not handle the run support very well. He walked a hitter in each of the first four innings and threw 69 pitches. But the Rays scored only one run.
Yandy Diaz walked leading off the bottom of the first, advanced to third on a double by Jonathan Aranda, and scored on Junior Caminero’s groundout.
Suarez was done after 5⅔ innings and 98 pitches, leaving the game with a runner at second. Wyatt Olds walked Liam Hicks and Victor Mesa Jr. on 12 pitches to load the bases.
He fell behind Jake Fraley 3 and 1, then came back to strike him out swinging through a fastball at the top of the strike zone. Olds threw up his hands after finally ending the inning. It wasn’t an elegant outing, but it was ultimately an effective one.
Greg Weissert worked around a two-out double by Caminero in the seventh inning to keep the lead at three runs, then came back for a 1-2-3 eighth.
Peter Abraham can be reached at peter.abraham@globe.com. Follow him on Bluesky at peteabeglobe.bsky.social.

item.title: [Boston Herald] Roman Anthony’s big game puts Red Sox on precipice of clinching playoff bid
item.dc:creator: Mac Cerullo
item.description: Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic. Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs. With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at
item.content:encoded:
Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic.
Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs.
With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at three entering the night, will drop to either one or two depending on the outcome of Friday’s late game between the Rangers and Blue Jays.
A Rangers win would mean the Red Sox could clinch with a win on Saturday, while a Blue Jays win would necessitate a win and a Blue Jays loss.
Following a string of poor offensive performances, Friday got off to a much stronger start at the plate. Roman Anthony put the Red Sox in front with a solo home run to lead off the game, and after the Rays tied it up in the bottom half of the first, Anthony delivered again in the second with a go-ahead two-run single with the bases loaded off Rays starter Ian Seymour, an alumnus of St. John’s High School in Shrewsbury.
Anthony finished 2 for 4 with three RBI, and the Red Sox never looked back.
“Taking that first one is big,” Anthony told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “Any win you can get against a team like that it’s a great win, so it’s a great day.”
Anthony’s first-inning blast was smoked. Measured at 107.7 mph off the bat and traveling 438 feet, the solo home run to right field narrowly missed landing in Tropicana Field’s ray tank.
His two-run single in the second inning was hit even harder, coming off the bat at 108.7 mph. Anthony came through after Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the inning with singles, Isiah Kiner-Falefa moved them into scoring position with a sacrifice bunt and Nate Eaton walked to load the bases.
It was doubly encouraging given Anthony’s recent struggles at the plate. After a hot start coming off the injured list, the outfielder came into Friday batting just .137 with one extra base hit over his past 12 games.
“I’ve been grinding, but that’s the beauty of this team,” Anthony said. “You’re never down and you’re never out.”
Jahmai Jones capped off the early offense with a solo shot to lead off the top of the third.
Tampa Bay scored its early run in the first after Yandy Diaz drew a leadoff walk, advanced to third on a Jonathan Aranda double and scored on a Junior Caminero groundout. But that was all the damage the Rays could do against Ranger Suarez, who allowed one run over 5 2/3 innings while falling one out short of his third consecutive quality start.
Suarez was uncharacteristically wild, walking five batters, but he limited the damage by allowing just three hits while striking out five.
The walks almost cost the Red Sox in the sixth inning.
Still leading by three, Suarez issued his fifth and final walk to lead off the sixth before recording two quick outs to finish his outing. But Wyatt Olds came on and immediately walked the first two men he faced, loading the bases and bringing the go-ahead run to the plate.
A brief mound visit followed, and Olds dug deep and struck out pinch hitter Jake Fraley to escape the inning unscathed.
“It was a weird game all the way around, we walked nine in total, Ranger walked five but still almost completed six innings and he was very competitive with men on base,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in St. Petersburg. “He lost some counts and behind more counts today, but he was able to make really good pitches with people on base.”
Walks put the Red Sox in one more jam in the bottom of the ninth inning.
With Aroldis Chapman unavailable with a lat issue and Garrett Whitlock having pitched on Thursday, Erik Miller took the mound in the ninth and walked three men. He allowed a run to score on a Victor Mesa Jr. groundout, and the third walk to Caminero brought the winning run to the plate with two outs.
Miller struck out Ryan Vilade, but the ball got away from Connor Wong and the Rays batter reached safely to extend the game and load the bases. But Miller fought back and drew a game-ending groundout from Chandler Simpson, leaving the Rays 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position and 12 men left on base in spite of the nine walks issued by the Red Sox pitching staff.
While Miller has now walked seven batters over his last 3 1/3 innings, Tracy said he felt the left-hander looked much better on Friday despite all of the traffic.
“I thought he was way more competitive,” Tracy said. “Everything was around the zone, stuff was good, he was getting some swing and miss like he usually does so I take a lot of good out of that outing.”
The win marked Boston’s first at Tropicana Field this season, and the club hopes plenty more will follow in the days and weeks to come. The Rays have long been in the driver’s seat for the AL East title, and barring a complete collapse over the final week Tampa Bay should soon lock down the American League’s top seed and a bye to the divisional round.
That means if the Red Sox (84-70) can get past the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series, they’d be headed right back to St. Petersburg to face the Rays in a rematch of the 2021 ALDS.
But first, the Red Sox hope to pop some bottles in the Tropicana Field visitor’s clubhouse before they fly back to Boston. First pitch on Saturday is scheduled for 4:10 p.m.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Insert Jahmai Jones into Lineup Against Rays Lefty
The Boston Red Sox placed designated hitter Jahmai Jones in the third spot in the starting lineup on Friday against Tampa Bay Rays left-hander Ian Seymour at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
According to MLB.com, Jones sits in the heart of the order between outfielders Roman Anthony and Wilyer Abreu. Shortstop Trevor Story and first baseman Nick Sogard also feature in the top five positions for Boston.
Left-hander Ranger Suárez gets the start on the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay's Seymour. Seymour enters the contest holding a 9-6 record with a 4.27 ERA and 150 strikeouts on the season, according to official team statistics.
Boston manager Chad Tracy opted to stack the right-handed hitting Jones near the top of the batting order due to ongoing injuries and lack of availability among several key players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Masataka Yoshida, Curtis Mead, and Willson Contreras.
According to MLB Trade Rumors, Boston acquired Jones off waivers on July 14 after the Detroit Tigers designated him for assignment, sending pitching prospect Jojo Ingrassia to Detroit as compensation.
Jones struggled with Detroit this season, batting .137 with a .221 slugging percentage across 105 plate appearances before his release. However, he has turned his season around in Boston, slashing .362/.464/.681 with three home runs and eight RBIs in 56 plate appearances.
Friday marks the 20th time overall this season that Jones has occupied the third spot in a starting lineup, having done so 19 times prior across his stints with Detroit and Boston. In those previous 35 plate appearances in the third spot, he posted a .219 batting average and a .661 OPS.
According to FanGraphs, the platoon splits support Boston's heavy usage of Jones against left-handed pitching. Across 138 plate appearances against lefties this year, Jones has recorded a .223 batting average, a .333 on-base percentage, and a .420 slugging percentage with five home runs, 15 walks, and 14 RBIs.
Conversely, Jones has registered just a .130 average in 23 at-bats against right-handed pitchers, with all five of his home runs this season coming exclusively against left-handers. He previously hit a two-run home run off Seymour during a July 18 matchup at Fenway Park.
Boston enters the three-game series against the American League East-leading Rays with an 83-70 record, holding the second AL Wild Card position and a five-game lead over the Cleveland Guardians. NESN reports Boston's magic number to clinch a postseason berth stands at three with nine games remaining on their schedule.

item.content:encoded:
La temporada regular de la MLB 2026 entra en su recta final y la pelea por los boletos a los Playoffs comienza a tomar forma. En medio de esta definición, varios peloteros mexicanos y mexicoamericanos mantienen vivas sus aspiraciones de llegar a la postemporada con sus respectivas organizaciones.
En la Liga Americana hay nombres que ya tienen prácticamente asegurado el escenario de octubre, mientras que otros todavía deben afrontar una intensa batalla por los puestos de comodín. Entre ellos aparecen jugadores que han tenido un papel importante durante la campaña y que buscan convertirse en representantes de México durante los Playoffs.
¿Qué mexicanos ya tienen encaminado su boleto?
Entre los jugadores que tienen su lugar asegurado destaca Jonathan Aranda, infielder tijuanense de los Tampa Bay Rays, franquicia que matemáticamente consiguió su clasificación a la postemporada y que se mantiene en la parte alta de la División Este de la Liga Americana.
Otro nombre que se encuentra en plena pelea es Jarren Durán, jardinero mexicoamericano de los Boston Red Sox. El pelotero forma parte de una novena que pelea por mantenerse en la zona de clasificación del joven circuito y que apunta a disputar la Serie de Comodines si consigue sostener su posición.
Por su parte, Alejandro Kirk continúa siendo una de las principales referencias mexicanas en las Grandes Ligas. El receptor de los Toronto Blue Jays afronta con su equipo una cerrada lucha por ingresar a los Playoffs de la Liga Americana, con cada partido de la recta final teniendo un peso importante en sus aspiraciones.
La pelea también está en la Liga Nacional
En el Viejo Circuito también hay varios peloteros con posibilidades de disputar la postemporada. Alek Thomas, jardinero mexicoamericano de los Arizona Diamondbacks, se encuentra involucrado en la cerrada pelea por los últimos boletos de comodín de la Liga Nacional.
Los San Diego Padres también cuentan con representación mexicana con Jeremiah Estrada, relevista mexicoamericano que forma parte del bullpen de una organización que se mantiene en puestos que actualmente entregarían un boleto a la postemporada mediante el comodín.
Mientras tanto, Javier Assad vive una situación favorable con los Chicago Cubs. El pitcher tijuanense forma parte de una novena que tiene prácticamente encaminada su clasificación, con los Cachorros ubicados en una posición privilegiada dentro de la carrera por los Playoffs de la Liga Nacional.
Otros jugadores también permanecen atentos a la definición de la temporada. Taijuan Walker, con los Philadelphia Phillies, así como JoJo Romero y Ramón Urías, con los St. Louis Cardinals, buscan mantener a sus respectivos equipos dentro de la conversación por los últimos lugares disponibles en la Nacional.

item.content:encoded:
La temporada 2026 de las Grandes Ligas entra en su tramo definitivo y la carrera por el Cy Young de la Liga Nacional comienza a tomar forma. Mientras algunos lanzadores todavía buscan cerrar fuerte para meterse en la conversación, Jacob Misiorowski ha conseguido separarse del resto gracias a una campaña en la que ha mostrado un nivel sobresaliente con los Milwaukee Brewers.
¿Por qué Jacob Misiorowski es el favorito al Cy Young?
Misiorowski ha sido particularmente consistente durante 2026 y encabeza a los pitchers abridores de MLB en varias categorías relevantes. Su dominio incluso se ha mantenido durante el último tramo de la campaña, una situación que ha fortalecido sus argumentos de cara al premio.
Durante agosto, el lanzador de los Brewers registró una efectividad de 2.32, cifra que representó su segundo peor registro mensual de toda la temporada. Su peor mes fue abril, cuando terminó con 3.58 de efectividad, lo que refleja la regularidad que ha mantenido conforme avanzó el calendario.
Uno de los lanzadores que todavía puede competir por el reconocimiento es Cristopher Sánchez, de los Philadelphia Phillies. El zurdo fue considerado uno de los principales favoritos al inicio de la carrera después de encadenar 50 entradas y dos tercios sin permitir carrera entre finales de abril y principios de junio. Aunque posteriormente perdió algo de terreno, sus números lo mantienen como un contendiente relevante.
Sánchez, de 29 años, lidera MLB en victorias con una marca de 16-4 y además presume una efectividad de 2.52, WHIP de 1.19 y 202 ponches en 175.1 entradas. Su desempeño lo mantiene dentro de la conversación, aunque ahora deberá aprovechar las últimas semanas de la temporada para intentar recortar distancia.
Otro nombre que aparece entre los contendientes es Chris Sale, de los Atlanta Braves. El veterano zurdo cuenta con experiencia y argumentos suficientes para mantenerse en la disputa, aunque Misiorowski ha conseguido colocarse por delante del grupo gracias al dominio mostrado a lo largo de la campaña.
Yoshinobu Yamamoto, el caballo negro
Yoshinobu Yamamoto representa una alternativa que no puede descartarse. El japonés se ha convertido en una pieza constante de la rotación de los Los Angeles Dodgers y sus números reflejan el nivel que ha alcanzado durante su segunda temporada en las Grandes Ligas.
Después de 24 aperturas, Yamamoto tiene marca de 12-8, efectividad de 2.56 y un espectacular WHIP de 0.89. Además, suma 153 ponches y únicamente 36 bases por bolas en 158 entradas de trabajo. Son estadísticas que en otras temporadas podrían colocarlo directamente entre los favoritos.

item.title: [MLB.com] Positive news on Contreras, Chapman tops list of injury updates
item.dc:creator: Ian Browne

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG – As they head into the final 10 days of the regular season, the Red Sox are monitoring a plethora of injuries to key players.
Given that the Sox still hold firm possession of the second American League Wild Card spot and could clinch a berth as early as this weekend, the plan will be to operate conservatively in hopes of getting everyone healthy for the games that count the most.
Here is an update on where things stand with those key players.
First baseman Willson Contreras
There was a big scare on Thursday night in Texas when the team’s most productive hitter this season was pelted on the top of his right hand with a pitch in the top of the eighth and immediately exited the game. Contreras said that in the moment, it felt like a fracture. Fortunately, X-rays taken at the ballpark were negative.
While interim manager Chad Tracy mentioned the possibility of follow-up imaging, there was none on Friday. Contreras didn’t have his hand taped and spent his share of time in the training room.
Where do things stand?
“Obviously, sore with some swelling,” Tracy said. “So nothing new other than just over the next couple of days, they'll work on treatment, on getting the swelling out, see if he can get grip strength back, and then we'll go from there. So just day to day.”
Could there still be additional scans?
“Not right now. Right now, with the initial one, they're optimistic,” said Tracy. “Just work on the swelling and see how he progresses over the next couple days, and then determine if they feel like they need more. But right now, they're just going to work on that.”
Closer Aroldis Chapman
When Garrett Whitlock closed Thursday’s win in Texas, it was obvious something was up with Chapman. It turns out he has been dealing with lat tightness he sustained while working out prior to Tuesday’s game.
Chapman downplayed the injury on Friday, saying the team is being conservative and that he felt healthy enough to play catch before the opener of the three-game series against the Rays. The Red Sox told him not to.
The lefty fireballer said he won’t pitch this weekend, but he expects to return during the final homestand, which starts on Tuesday.
“I’m not worried at all,” Chapman said. “From the first time I felt it to today, I feel very good. I was going to go out and throw, but the team wants to take it slow, and they want me to take my time.“
It is all about being 100% for the first game of the playoffs on Sept. 29, right?
“Yeah, of course,” said Chapman. “A hundred percent.”
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela
Boston’s All-Star center fielder hasn’t played since Sept. 2 due to a right quad strain. It sounds unlikely he’ll be able to play in a rehab game for Triple-A Worcester because that season ends on Sunday. But Tracy is confident with where Rafaela is at.
“I think he got close to 90% of his acceleration yesterday,” said Tracy. “So not ready yet, but he's moving quickly in the right direction, which is good. If he doesn’t play [for Worcester], there is a goal of getting him some live at-bats of some kind. You know, like live BP-type at-bats of some kind, plus the Trajekt. The important thing is that the running piece keeps going in the right direction.”
Left-hander Garrett Crochet
Boston’s ace, who has been out since April 25 due to a left shoulder injury, is still racing against the clock to try to pitch in relief during the postseason. His next step will be on Saturday, when he throws his second up-and-down bullpen session of the week at Fenway Park.
For Crochet to have any shot at pitching at the start of the postseason, he would have to start facing hitters by next week.
“I would say we're to the point where these next five days or so are going to be pretty telling,” said Tracy. “How does the side go, and what can we do with him early next week? And that'll give us a better idea of the answer to that question.”
Right-hander Tanner Houck
The righty will make the fourth and final appearance of his Minor League rehab assignment when he throws roughly 50 pitches for Worcester on Saturday. It’s possible Houck will get a tuneup or two in regular-season action for the Red Sox next week, which could give the club a better gauge if he’s a possibility to pitch in the playoffs. Houck had Tommy John surgery 13 months ago.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox Get Excellent Injury News on Ceddanne Rafaela Ahead of Postseason originally appeared on NESN. Add NESN as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Boston Red Sox's injuries have been unfortunate for much of this season, and it doesn't really feel like things will change at this point.
Unfortunately for the Red Sox, they aren't guaranteed to get many of these guys healthy before the postseason.
Ultimately, the Red Sox have to hope things work out in the injury department and go from there. One player who is currently missed more than most others is Ceddanne Rafaela, who injured his quadriceps during a Sept. 2 game against the Seattle Mariners.
Rafaela has yet to play since the injury but was one of the better players in this Red Sox lineup. He was hitting .282 with 32 doubles and playing elite outfield defense.
According to the latest report, while it remains uncertain when he'll return, he's getting some work in, which is a positive sign.
"Rafaela (quadriceps) is with Triple-A Worcester on Thursday and will do some hitting off their Trajekt machine, Tommy Cassell of the Worcester Telegram & Gazette reports.
"It's unclear what the next steps for Rafaela will be, but he could play in some rehab games for Worcester before rejoining Boston's active roster. The center fielder has not played in more than two weeks as he works his way back from a right quadriceps strain," CBS wrote.
The rehab games are where things get interesting here.
The Red Sox only have about a week and a half of regular-season games left, so if Rafaela has to play in a few Triple-A games, there is a scenario in which he doesn't return to Boston before the expected Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees, if that's how things fall.

item.title: [Newsday] Yankees' Cam Schlittler would appear to be the front-runner for the American League Cy Young Award

item.content:encoded:
By any objective measure, Cam Schlittler, in his first full season in the majors, is having one of the best seasons any Yankees starter has ever had.
Schlittler, who is expected to start Saturday against the Diamondbacks in Phoenix, is 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA. Those numbers alone, however, don’t tell the full story of Schlittler’s 2026 season, one that has established him as a co-favorite, along with Dylan Cease of the Blue Jays, for the American League Cy Young Award.
After Schlittler threw six scoreless innings Sunday afternoon in a 2-0 victory over the Mets, manager Aaron Boone even made a push for him to be considered for another award.
“He might be the MVP, too,” Boone said. “It’s been awesome. Just an awesome season.”
That, of course, is a long shot at best. Many voters, not to mention players, see the MVP as the sole dominion of position players, just as the Cy Young Award is reserved for pitchers.
“He’s definitely pitching like an MVP,” Aaron Judge said after Sunday's win. “They’ve got a Cy Young Award for a reason — best pitcher in the game. He’s got my vote definitely for the Cy Young.”
Regardless, Schlittler is in the midst of a strong finishing kick to his year, and it is not a stretch to say he has emerged as the favorite with just over a week left in the regular season.
Though Schlittler has the edge over Cease in many of the numbers — traditional as well as what would be considered more “modern” ones — used when it comes to evaluating pitchers for the Cy Young Award, Cease has some of those in his favor as well.
Digging into many of those numbers, all of them as of Wednesday afternoon:
Schlittler is second in the American League in wins with 14 compared to 11 for Cease (11-6), though Cy Young Award voters have put little emphasis on wins in the last decade-plus.
The Mariners' Felix Hernandez, for instance, won the AL Cy Young Award in 2010 after going 13-12 (with an MLB-leading 2.27 ERA, one of many statistics, both old-school and new-school, in which he led). The Mets' Jacob deGrom won the NL award in 2018 after going 10-9 (with an MLB-best 1.70 ERA and dominating pretty much every other statistical category), and the Pirates' Paul Skenes took NL honors last season after going 10-10 (with an MLB-leading 1.97 ERA and widespread statistical dominance elsewhere).
Cease pitched against the Rangers on Friday night. Entering that game, Schlittler led him in ERA, 1.95 to 2.38; walks and hits per innings pitched (WHIP), 0.90 to 1.06; innings, 184 2/3 to 166 1/3, and Wins above Replacement, 7.0 to 6.1, according to baseball-reference.com, and 5.9 to 5.6, according to Fangraphs.com.
Schlittler also held the edge in ERA+, a statistic measuring the quality of a pitcher’s ERA compared to the league average, adjusting to the ballpark he pitches in, with the league average being 100.
Cease’s ERA+ was 185, a terrific, Cy Young Award-worthy number in many years, but this year it ranked him second in the AL to Schlittler’s extraordinary ERA+ of 216 (deGrom’s ERA+ in 2018 was 218, Skenes’ in 2025 was 226).
Schlittler's “calling card” from the time he was promoted to the big leagues in July 2025 has been command, according to Boone, and he dominates Cease in that category as well.
Despite pitching 18 1/3 more innings, Schlittler has walked only 44 batters to Cease's 72. Schlittler ranks fifth in the AL in walks per nine innings at 2.1 and Cease ranks 22nd at 3.9.
Cease does have some numbers in his favor.
Despite throwing 18 1/3 fewer innings, Cease had 236 strikeouts, tied for the MLB lead, to Schlittler’s 228, giving the former a ratio of 12.8 strikeouts per nine innings to the latter’s 11.1. Cease had 13 games with at least nine strikeouts, the most of any pitcher in the AL, and Schlittler has seven such games.
Cease has been slightly harder to hit, with opposing batters producing a .177 batting average against, which leads the AL among qualified starting pitchers, compared to a .185 batting average against for Schlittler (which ranks him second in that category). Entering Friday, Cease was allowing 5.7 hits per nine innings and Schlittler is allowing 6.0.
Cease had allowed only 11 homers in his 166 1/3 innings and Schlittler has allowed 16 in his 184 2/3 innings.
Cease also holds the edge over Schlittler in Fielding Independent Pitching (FIP), which attempts to measure a pitcher’s performance based on those elements he directly controls before a ball is put in play and the vagaries of defense become a factor. Those would be strikeouts, walks, homers allowed and hit batsmen.
Cease led the AL in FIP at 2.48. Schlittler is second at 2.57.
Though Cease does hold an advantage in some of the difficulty-to-hit categories, they likely won’t be enough — at the moment, anyway — to deny Schlittler's bid to become the seventh Yankee to win a Cy Young Award (Gerrit Cole was the most recent in 2023).
And there’s this: Schlittler’s closing argument has been especially eye-popping. He’s allowed one run or fewer in an MLB-leading (and franchise-record) 21 starts this season, including in each of his last seven starts, going 4-0 with a 1.00 ERA and a 0.76 WHIP in that span. He has a 0.81 ERA and 0.72 WHIP in those 21 games. In two other games, he allowed zero or one earned run.
Schlittler has allowed three or fewer runs in 27 of his 31 starts and two or fewer in 24 of them.
Cease had 16 outings in which he allowed one run or fewer, certainly an impressive number, but had not pitched quite as well of late, 4-0 with a 2.70 ERA in his previous seven outings.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Willson Contreras' frustrations following hit by pitch are a brewing Red Sox problem
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello
item.description: Willson Contreras played a key role in the Boston Red Sox's come-from-behind win in the series finale against the Texas Rangers, but not in a way he would have preferred. Contreras was plunked in the hand by struggling Rangers reliever Jakob Junis in the top of the eighth, setting the scene for Trevor Story to launch a go-ahead three-run homer off All-Star closer Jacob Latz. The good news is that Contreras underwent x-rays following the game, and they came back clean. The veteran didn't seem to
item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras played a key role in the Boston Red Sox's come-from-behind win in the series finale against the Texas Rangers, but not in a way he would have preferred. Contreras was plunked in the hand by struggling Rangers reliever Jakob Junis in the top of the eighth, setting the scene for Trevor Story to launch a go-ahead three-run homer off All-Star closer Jacob Latz.
The good news is that Contreras underwent x-rays following the game, and they came back clean. The veteran didn't seem to agree with the diagnosis, saying that it felt like a fracture and that he's fractured that hand before and experienced some numbness. More importantly, he's frustrated.
“If nobody does anything about it, I’m going to keep getting hit. That’s the way I see it. That’s it,” Contreras said, via Tim Healey of The Boston Globe.
Contreras has been hit by a pitch 24 times this season, third-most in the league. Of course, he also crowds the plate more than almost any hitter in the game. You want to claim the entire plate as your own; expect opposing pitchers to try and prove to you that the inside corner is, in fact, theirs.
By the sound of it, that is lost on Contreras. It seems as if the former St. Louis Cardinal wants one of Boston's pitchers to go out and start beaning batters in retaliation. That might be how things were done in the olden days, but now that's a recipe for escalation, a potential brawl, and possible suspensions.
Given that he doesn't feel as if any of the hurlers have come to his defense, it's likely that won't change. These bad feelings could become a cause for concern, and even more so with us approaching October's doorstep.
Willson Contreras could be threatening Red Sox chemistry again with latest HBP outrage
On the field, Contreras has had a fantastic first season in Boston. His 27 homers are already a career high, and if it holds, his .387 on-base percentage will be a career-best, too. Meanwhile, his .518 slugging percentage is the second-best mark of his career. There was a reason why he was voted a top AL MVP contender in an MLB.com poll at the end of August.
That's been great, but there have been issues. Contreras made some confusing comments after Alex Cora was dismissed, seemingly taking a shot at the team's young players in the process. He has also gotten into it with fans after being booed for not running out a ground ball back in August, further cementing his reputation as a prickly player.
At the same time, before the tide turned on the Red Sox's season and trade rumors enveloped him, he stated that he wouldn't waive his no-trade clause, desiring to finish his career in Boston.
Overall, it's odd. At times, it has seemed as if he doesn't really want to be here, despite his protest that, in fact, Boston is the only place he envisions himself playing.
This latest incident is more dangerous. Who knows what is said behind closed doors, but hurt bodies and hurt feelings don't go well together. If Contreras pushes the "defense" issue, it could cause a real rift. The pitchers could side with each other, while the hitters rally around Contreras.
The lines could also be different if there are enough players on either side of the positional divide with a more updated view of bean ball, so that different cliques could form.
The Red Sox have bigger issues at hand right now. They're going to have to figure out their postseason roster crunch. They're hoping that Aroldis Chapman's sore lat isn't anything serious. They need to find a way to get Roman Anthony's bat going before the playoffs begin. What they don't have time for is Contreras getting in his feelings because he got hit while standing on top of the plate.

item.content:encoded:
RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the latest on a number of key injured Red Sox players. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
Ahead of the Boston Red Sox series opener at Tropicana Field against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, interim manager Chad Tracy met with the media and provided updates on a number of injured Red Sox players.
Here's what you need to know:
All eyes were on the All-Star first baseman after Thursday night's win over the Texas Rangers. Contreras exited the game in the eighth inning after being hit by a pitch on the right-hand. According to MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, Contreras told reporters after the game that the injury "felt" like a fracture. While initial X-Rays were negative, as the team learned with infielder Curtis Mead, that doesn't mean Contreras was completely out of the woods yet. According to MLB.com's Ian Browne, the team is waiting for swelling in the 34-year-old's hand to subside before testing his grip strength to determine if additional testing is needed.
Contreras is out of the lineup for Friday's series opener.
Crochet threw a 30-pitch up-and-down bullpen session on Tuesday back at Fenway Park, representing the most labor-intensive of the four throwing sessions the 27-year-old has done since restarting a throwing progression Aug. 3. According to WEEI's Rob Bradford, Crochet will throw another side session on Saturday as he continues to work his way back from left shoulder inflammation that has kept him out since April 29.
After turning to Garrett Whitlock to lock down Thursday's win, Tracy told reporters, including Cotillo, that Chapman was unavailable with LAT tightness. According to Bradford, Chapman said the injury popped up ahead of Tuesday's series opener in Texas and that he wasn't concerned about the injury, saying the latest he would return to the mound would be during the team's upcoming home stand, beginning on Tuesday night, if he doesn't make an appearance in Tampa.
Tyron Guerrero
After landing on the injured list on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The 35-year-old flamethrower was expected to be activated when he was first eligible, ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas. However, after experiencing lower back tightness, the team delayed his activation. According to Bradford, Guerrero "felt fine" after throwing 20 pitches off the mound on Friday afternoon. However, it still remains unclear when he may be activated.
The 32-year-old outfielder landed on the injured list last Friday with a "right foot ligament injury" after getting it caught in the grates along the center field wall in the Sept. 8 loss to the Los Angeles Angels. As Bradford noted, White has been diagnosed with a ligament tear, likely ending his season.
White's injury seems to open the door for Spring Training standout Braiden Ward to join the Red Sox as a fourth outfielder/pinch runner in the playoffs.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to carry the momentum from Thursday's come-from-behind win into the final road series of the year against the Rays. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) will get the start for the Red Sox opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for the Rays. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Willson Contreras Injury Update Hints Red Sox Avoided Serious Issue
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: The Boston Red Sox will not have Willson Contreras in the lineup on Friday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, but there is hope for the All-Star slugger after an early exit on Thursday night. Contreras had to leave the club's series finale against the Texas Rangers on Thursday night after getting hit by a pitch on his hand. At the time, it was reported that his X-rays came back negative, but there was still some fear. Contreras himself spoke about the injury and said that it felt like a fracture
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox will not have Willson Contreras in the lineup on Friday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, but there is hope for the All-Star slugger after an early exit on Thursday night.
Contreras had to leave the club's series finale against the Texas Rangers on Thursday night after getting hit by a pitch on his hand. At the time, it was reported that his X-rays came back negative, but there was still some fear. Contreras himself spoke about the injury and said that it felt like a fracture while citing the fact that he previously had one.
Now, of course, it would've been great to see Contreras in Boston's lineup on Friday, but he hasn't been ruled out for the weekend and Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that no new scans are currently planned, as shared on X by MassLive.com's Sean McAdam.
Willson Contreras Update
"Willson Contreras is out of the lineup, giving his hand some time to recover. Chad Tracy wouldn’t rule him out for the weekend, but Sox are being cautious. No new scans planned," McAdam wrote on X.
Again, it would've been great to see Contreras back in the lineup, but there are positives to take away from this update. First and foremost, the fact that more scans aren't currently planned is a sign of confidence from the club. Think back to Curtis Mead, for example. When he got hit on the wrist in his first game as a member of the Red Sox, his X-rays initially came back as negative. Then, the next day, it was shared that he actually had suffered a fractured wrist.
At this point, every time someone gets hit by a pitch on the wrist/hand, it immediately makes fans think about Mead. This process with Contreras is much more positive than it was with Mead. The fact that almost 24 hours later, the club hasn't ruled him out for the weekend and doesn't have more tests planned is a very good sign that he simply is dealing with a bruise, or something of that nature.
Boston needs Contreras if it wants to make a run this season. Things are wide open in the American League, especially in the wake of Aaron Judge being placed on the Injured List for the New York Yankees. Boston, New York and Tampa Bay are the top three contenders in the American League and with New York hurting, the top two contenders should be the Red Sox and the Rays. If Contreras returns over the weekend, Boston is going to be just fine.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox secured a major 4-3 victory over the Texas Rangers on Thursday night in their series finale, avoiding the sweep.
On Friday, they’ll start a weekend series against the American League-best Tampa Bay Rays, and ahead of the opener, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy made a notable lineup decision involving All-Star Willson Contreras after a pitch hit him on the hand Thursday.
Red Sox Announce Contreras Decision
X-rays came back negative after Thursday’s game on Contreras’ hand, fortunately. However, he is not in the starting lineup for the opener against Tampa Bay.
Starting at first base in place of Contreras will be Nick Sogard, who will bat second in the order behind leadoff hitter Roman Anthony.
Stepping into the three and four holes will be designated hitter Jahmai Jones and outfielder Wilyer Abreu.
Here’s the full Red Sox lineup:
Via Underdog MLB: “Red Sox 9/18 R. Anthony LF N. Sogard 1B J. Jones DH W. Abreu RF T. Story SS C. Durbin 3B I. Kiner-Falefa 2B N. Eaton CF C. Wong C R. Suarez SP.”

Contreras’ 2026 Season
In his first year with the Red Sox, Contreras has appeared in 129 games and recorded 68 runs, 123 hits, 27 home runs, and 81 RBIs across 446 at-bats while batting .276 with a .518 slugging percentage and a .905 OPS.
Looking at the Red Sox
Boston enters Friday night with an 83-70 overall record and sits on the verge of clinching a postseason bid. If they clinch, they’ll enter the playoffs as the second Wild Card team.
If the current standings hold, the Red Sox would travel to the Bronx to face the New York Yankees in a best-of-three Wild Card series.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Aroldis Chapman injury news is the last thing Red Sox’s already-strained bullpen needs

After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was
item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox fans were already going through it on Thursday night after Willson Contreras left the series finale against the Texas Rangers early after being hit by a pitch on the hand. Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse.
Whitlock is no slouch, as Red Sox fans know, and he got through the ninth frame unscathed, but fans expect to see Aroldis Chapman in moments like that. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was unavailable due to a lat issue.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said in his September 17 postgame presser that Chapman has been dealing with lat tightness for a couple of days but that he's been improving lately. Boston has classified him as day-to-day and it will routinely check on his recovery progress to gauge his availability.
The best news from Tracy on Chapman is that the team will not place him on the injured list. The Sox's bullpen has been one of their deadliest weapons all season and Chapman with his 1.95 ERA, 34 saves, blistering velocity and unmatched consistency at 38 years old has been a huge part of that success.
Aroldis Chapman injury news is a blow the Red Sox's bullpen can't afford as the playoffs near
Still, having Chapman at anything less than 100 percent is dangerous this late in the season with the playoffs on the horizon. In a tight game, one slip-up in the ninth inning could lead to disaster.
The rest of the Red Sox's bullpen is hardly in its best shape. Justin Slaten's season ended following continued flexor issues and Tyron Guerrero is still on the IL bouncing back from shoulder inflammation. Erik Miller is also dealing with a mechanical issue that has severely impacted his command over his last two outings.
If Chapman's injury is as mild as Tracy is letting on and he doesn't need an IL stint, Boston might be able to avoid disaster. But it also needs Chapman's help to clinch its playoff spot in the first place. The offense is struggling to get out to enough of a lead that it doesn't need Chapman to hold a slim margin in the late innings, but that won't fly in the postseason, especially with an injured closer.
At least the Red Sox expect some relief reinforcements in the coming days. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working towards returns from long-term injuries in a relief role and they could take some pressure off the 'pen, but neither could fill Chapman's role.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] Trevor Story's game-winning home run vs. Rangers is a reminder of his under-the-radar Red Sox role
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: The Boston Red Sox seem to be stalling out at the worst possible time. The offense has had trouble limiting strikeouts, advancing runners and hitting, in general with a clinching opportunity on the line. But under the doom and gloom of the rest of the offense, there is hidden a triumphant return from injury by an unexpected player: Trevor Story. He played hero on September 17 against the Texas Rangers with an eighth-inning, three-run homer to stave off a sweep and help his team inch closer to cl
item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox seem to be stalling out at the worst possible time. The offense has had trouble limiting strikeouts, advancing runners and hitting, in general with a clinching opportunity on the line.
But under the doom and gloom of the rest of the offense, there is hidden a triumphant return from injury by an unexpected player: Trevor Story. He played hero on September 17 against the Texas Rangers with an eighth-inning, three-run homer to stave off a sweep and help his team inch closer to clinching a playoff berth.
Even before that, Story had been hitting well while the rest of Boston's bats have faltered, including some of its best, like Willson Contreras and Roman Anthony (subscription required). Story is slashing .349/.359/.508 with seven doubles, a home run and nine RBI since he returned from the injured list on August 30. Boston's lineup hasn't been long enough lately to make the best of its minimal offensive production, so Story's efforts have gone under-the-radar.
There's quite a bit of swing and miss in Story's game, as there always has been. He's fanned at a 31.3 percent clip in the 16 games he's played since coming off the IL, which hasn't helped Boston's strikeout totals each game. But Story got the job done when the Sox needed him most, and for that he deserves credit.
Trevor Story has been a bright spot in Red Sox's offense throughout September slump
The Red Sox have looked utterly lifeless at the plate and Story was able to break through the ugly spell. With any luck, his game-saver from Thursday night will inspire his teammates to free themselves from whatever late-season funk they're in, which has delayed their clinching ceremony enough already.
It's reassuring to see Story get hot with just a few series remaining. He also performed exceptionally well last September with a .302/.337/.458 slash line, six doubles, three home runs and 12 RBI over 22 games that month. He's looking like a weapon en-route to a Wild Card matchup for the second year in a row.
Story has also seemingly crushed the slump he was in when the season started. The shortstop batted only .206/.244/.303 with 57 strikeouts to just eight walks over 41 games before his injury. Before Story and the Red Sox revealed the sports hernia bugging the infielder, fans were under the impression that another rough year was coming, but pain from the injury might've severely hampered his play.
After Boston went without signing a true slugger over the offseason (a Pete Alonso or Kyle Schwarber type, a more consistent home run hitter than Contreras), it needed Story to build off his 2025 season for the offense to be at its best. There hasn't been much power in Story's game yet, but maybe his game-saving homer against the Rangers changes the tides. Story has been one of few bright spots this month in the Red Sox's underachieving offense and the rest of the team needs to play closer to his level to maintain its Wild Card standing as the regular season draws to a close.

item.content:encoded:
Alec Gamboa, who played for the Lotte Giants in the KBO League last year. He failed to re-sign with Lotte, but a year later he debuted in the major leagues and is aiming to make the postseason roster.
On the 18th (Korean time) at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, in the game against the Texas Rangers, Gamboa came in with one out in the eighth inning and no runners on, recorded 2/3 of an inning, allowed one hit and no runs, and earned a hold. It was his second hold of the season.
That day Gamboa entered the game after Trevor Story hit a go-ahead three-run homer in the top of the eighth to put them up 4-3. Starter Sonny Gray pitched well with 6 1/3 innings, three hits (one home run), three walks, six strikeouts and three runs, and second pitcher Wyatt Alls recorded one inning, one strikeout and no runs.
Gamboa came in to face a left-handed batting lineup of Corey Seager and Josh Young. He gave up a single to the first batter, Seager, to right field. Later, he fell behind Josh Young 3-1 in the count but induced a shortstop grounder with a low 95.6-mph sinker, producing a double play to end the inning.
After recording his first hold in his debut by getting Lee Jung-hoo and others out in the Aug. 22 game against the San Francisco Giants, he recorded his second hold of the season. Gamboa's season performance is excellent. In 19 appearances he pitched 29 2/3 innings with 1 win, 2 holds, 1 save, a 1.21 ERA, a .216 batting average against and a 1.04 WHIP.
That day closer Aroldis Chapman could not take the mound because of trapezius muscle stiffness, and another lefty in the high-leverage group, Eric Miller, had earlier shown instability on the 17th against Texas by allowing three runs on 22 pitches in one inning. As a result, rookie right-hander Wyatt Alls and left-hander Gamboa had to take on the high-leverage roles, and setup man Garrett Whitlock had to assume the closer role. All of them then held the one-run lead.
Acting manager Chad Tracy praised Alls and Gamboa's high-leverage performances, saying, "They were really great. They were inserted suddenly into important situations. At times they had to take the mound with the lead, and they did really well."
Gamboa once again successfully passed a high-leverage test for the high-leverage group. Now the question is whether he can join Boston's postseason journey. Boston has a 83-70 record and sits second in the wild-card standings. They are five games ahead of the third-place Cleveland Guardians, so barring an upset they are all but certain to secure the 5 seed.
Over the Monster, which reports on Boston news, listed Gamboa in the "pitchers who need to prove themselves" spot while predicting the postseason roster. The outlet said, "He is a player who had a pleasantly surprising performance this year. He even made two starts as an opener. In recent weeks the bullpen has had injuries, and combined with his own performance, he has risen to the point of being used in higher-stakes, high-leverage situations."
Closers Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Eric Miller, Tyrone Guerrero and Garrett Crochet are confirmed. It is likely that one more left-handed reliever will be added and the rest filled with right-handers.
They went on to say, "If Aroldis Chapman, Eric Miller and Garrett Crochet are the confirmed left-handed bullpen pieces, the final left-handed spot could be a competition between Hobani Moran and Gamboa," and added, "If I had to pick the final four now, I would choose Brayan Bello, Tanner Houck, Moran and Gamboa," predicting they would make the postseason roster.
Boston regional outlet MassLive also highlighted the performances of Gamboa and Alls on the 17th, saying, "He seized an unexpected opportunity this year, expanded his standing, and his entry into the postseason roster race—which would have been hard to imagine just a few weeks ago—is worthy of high praise," introducing that Gamboa has performed well enough to be included on the postseason roster.
Gamboa was drafted by the Los Angeles Dodgers in the ninth round, 281st overall, in the 2019 draft. But he couldn't break through the Dodgers' deep minor league system, and last year he joined the KBO League's Lotte Giants as a replacement player and delivered a sensational performance.
He had an especially strong performance, including being named player of the month for June, but fatigue accumulated late in the season and elbow pain caused him to miss several turns in the rotation, preventing a smooth finish. His KBO League stats were 19 games, 108 innings, 7 wins, 8 losses and a 3.58 ERA.
Although Gamboa failed to re-sign with Lotte, he said of going to Lotte, "It was a good opportunity to show myself elsewhere. I wanted to experience a bigger and new environment than Triple-A in the U.S. I believed I would show good pitching there, return to the U.S. and seize another opportunity," and added, "Before going to Korea I had never been abroad. Experiencing another country, seeing how polite the people there are and how much they love baseball, and seeing what style of baseball they play was really fun," saying it was an opportunity that lifted his spirits.
Was failing to re-sign with Lotte a blessing in disguise? After signing a minor league deal with Boston he made an emotional big league debut and now stands on the verge of making the postseason roster. Gamboa is becoming a symbol of a life turnaround.
[OSEN]

Chapman downplayed his lat issue Friday, saying he's "not worried at all" about the injury and plans to pitch again during Boston's final regular-season homestand next week, Sean McAdam of MassLive.com reports.
Chapman said he first felt it Tuesday, and he's improved throughout the week. With Boston closing in on a playoff berth, the Red Sox will likely be conservative with their star closer. Garrett Whitlock filled in during the ninth inning of Thursday's 4-3 win over the Rangers, locking down his fourth save of the season. it sounds like Chapman will be unavailable for this weekend's set with the Rays.

Sonny Gray allowed three earned runs on three hits and three walks while striking out six over 6 1/3 innings in Thursday’s win over the Rangers.

Gray continues a solid stretch of late, allowing two earned runs or less in five of his last eight trips to the mound. item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Payton Tolle's Rookie Season Takes Historic Turn for Red Sox
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: Boston Red Sox flamethrower Payton Tolle made his big league debut in 2025 after a meteoric rise through the minors. He quickly made Boston fans fall in love with him because of his blistering fastball, and quirky personality. Last year, he made it into seven games in the majors. item.content:encoded:
Boston Red Sox flamethrower Payton Tolle made his big league debut in 2025 after a meteoric rise through the minors. He quickly made Boston fans fall in love with him because of his blistering fastball, and quirky personality.
Last year, he made it into seven games in the majors. This year, he didn't make the big league out of camp, but he was quickly promoted as injuries popped up elsewhere. Boston's fortunate it made the decision it did to give the lefty a shot because he has been incredible.
So far this season, he has made 25 starts as a rookie and has a 3.02 ERA and a 166-to-38 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 143 innings pitched. If that doesn't impress you enough, he actually is the only rookie in big league history to record a strikeout rate of 28 percent or more and a walk rate of seven percent or lower across at least 140 innings pitched, per Eric Cross of RotoBaller.
Payton Tolle Has Put Together A Historic Rookie Season
"Red Sox Payton Tolle is the only pitcher in MLB history to meet the three thresholds below in their rookie season: 140 innings pitched, strikeout rate above 28 percent, walk rate below 7 percent," Cross wrote.
Terms like "ace" and "No. 1 starter" get tossed around a lot. There aren't many true aces in baseball, or at least not as many as are talked about. While this is the case, Tolle clearly has that type of upside. This is a guy who is just 23 years old. His advanced metrics back up this idea that he can be a legit No. 1 ace.
Right now, he's in the 96th percentile in expected ERA, 93rd percentile in expected batting average against, 96th percentile in chase rate, 98th percentile in extension, 89th percentile in strikeout rate, 94th percentile in fastball run value and the 90th percentile in pitching run value, among many others.
Again, he wasn't even on the Red Sox's Opening Day roster. But he got his opportunity and he has shown clear growth. It has been known that he has an elite fastball. The biggest question for him coming into the 2026 season was whether or not he could develop his secondary pitches. He has done just that, which is a big reason for his overall success.
The Red Sox have a star on their hands, to say the least.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Boston Red Sox On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.content:encoded:
Cubs infielder Alex Bregman's horse wins at Churchill Downs, then gets claimed by new owners
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (AP) — Alex Bregman and his Chicago Cubs teammates celebrated the third baseman's horse winning a race at Churchill Downs.
It was short-lived, however, when the horse was claimed by new owners afterward.
Act of Parliament overcame a troubled start under jockey Axel Concepcion and rallied to win by three-quarters of a length on Thursday. The 3-year-old colt paid $8.68 to win.
"It was electric,” winning trainer Will Walden said. “To have Alex and the entire team here and then have the horse come through like that made it a pretty special night.”
The Cubs visited the historic Louisville track on their off day before opening a three-game set at Cincinnati on Friday.
Cubs MVP candidate Pete Crow-Armstrong delivered a pep talk to Act of Parliament in the paddock before the race. Cubs manager Craig Counsell led the colt into the winner's circle afterward.
Several Cubs rookies dressed in racing-themed costumes, including pitcher Ryan Rolison, who donned a horse costume, and Pedro Ramirez, who dressed as a jockey.
Bregman Family Racing, the ballplayer's stable, bought Act of Parliament for $65,000.
The colt earned $27,108 for his first career victory. But Bregman lost him in the claiming race.
Act of Parliament was claimed for $20,000 afterward in a random blind draw used to break a tie when six different owners submitted bids beforehand to buy the colt. He was then transferred to a new trainer.
___

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox open up a three-game series against AL East rival Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, September 18, at Tropicana Field.
Ranger Suarez will get the ball for Boston tonight. After that, the pitching plans are unclear. The Red Sox have listed TBDs for their starting pitcher spot on Saturday and Sunday, per Tim Healey of the Boston Globe. Payton Tolle and Patrick Sandoval were lined up to start this weekend, but that is now in doubt.
Probable pitchers for Red Sox-Rays this weekend…
* Friday: Ranger Suarez vs. Ian Seymour* Saturday: TBD vs. Freddy Peralta* Sunday: TBD vs. Griffin Jax
Saturday would be Payton Tolle's day, if the Red Sox stay on turn. We'll see how they handle it.
— Tim Healey (@timbhealey) September 17, 2026
Tolle has already zoomed past his previous career high in innings as a pro. The lefty tossed 108 frames between the minors and majors in 2025. Tolle has thrown 158 innings across both levels this season.
Boston Red Sox May Skip Payton Tolle Against the Tampa Bay Rays
Tolle has been a fixture in Boston's rotation for much of the season. He's posted a 3.03 ERA across 25 starts with the big-league club. The young lefty opened the season in the minors, but was promoted to the majors in April. Tolle has solidified a pitching staff that has dealt with injuries and underperformance at times in 2026.
While he won't win AL Rookie of the Year, Tolle has put together a solid case. He's right up there with Cleveland Guardians left-hander Parker Messick as the top rookie starter in the American League. Kevin McGonigle of the Detroit Tigers and Munetaka Murakami of the Chicago White Sox are the betting favorites, but Tolle and Messick will receive some down-ballot votes.
Tolle struggled to a 6.06 ERA in his first taste of the big leagues last year. He missed bats at a decent 25.7% clip, but notched a 10.8% walk rate. The lefty has improved in both departments this season. Tolle pushed his strikeout rate to 28.9% and trimmed his walk rate to 6.6% in his first full campaign as a major league starter.
Red Sox Lining Up Postseason Rotation
Moving Tolle's next start could be an effort to align the playoff rotation. The pitching staff will likely be headlined by Sonny Gray, but the second and third slots are up for grabs. Suarez has a solid case to pitch the second game of the Wild Card round. The gig could also go to Tolle.
Sandoval and Jake Bennett are likely looking at long relief roles in the first round of the playoffs. Both have had decent stretches this season, but faded recently. Bennett has permitted a dozen runs in three September starts. Sandoval has a 7.82 ERA this month.
Brayan Bello is the question mark among the unit. He's struggled as a starter and been tremendous out of the bullpen. Bello could operate in tandem with one of Boston's many left-handed starters.
